name: Five Elements of the City
summary: Lynch (1960). Cities are mentally legible through paths, edges, districts, nodes, and landmarks. The dominant cognitive framework for urban design.
sources: The Image of the City, K. Lynch, 1960

name: Eyes on the Street
summary: Jacobs (1961). Continuous informal surveillance from active ground floors, mixed uses, and visible windows is the foundation of urban safety.
sources: Death and Life of Great American Cities, J. Jacobs, 1961

name: Community of 7000
summary: Alexander Pattern 12. Cities should be subdivided into political communities of about 7,000, the largest size at which face-to-face self-governance is still viable.

name: Identifiable Neighborhood
summary: Alexander Pattern 14. Neighbourhoods should have identifiable boundaries, ~5,000 inhabitants, and ~300m diameter.

name: Activity Nodes
summary: Alexander Pattern 30. Concentrate community facilities so they reinforce each other; locate them at meeting points of natural movement.

name: Promenade
summary: Alexander Pattern 31. Every subculture needs a centre for its public life; the promenade is where people go to see and be seen.

name: Shopping Street
summary: Alexander Pattern 32. Linear pedestrianised commercial street ~150-300m long; shops on both sides; activity from morning to evening.

name: Green Streets
summary: Alexander Pattern 51. Local streets converted from asphalt to a mosaic of green: trees, gravel, flagstones; cars allowed but slow.

name: Main Gateways
summary: Alexander Pattern 53. Mark every transition between major neighbourhoods or districts with a clear physical gateway.

name: Small Public Squares
summary: Alexander Pattern 61. Public squares should be small — ~18m × 18m — to retain intimacy and life.

name: Positive Outdoor Space
summary: Alexander Pattern 106. Outdoor space should be partially enclosed, with definite positive shape — not the leftover space between buildings.

name: Activity Pockets
summary: Alexander Pattern 124. Surround public space with pockets of activity — small partly-enclosed areas at the edges that draw people in.
